contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: For one query, compare the entire legal strategy cost—including sorting, copying, predicate work, and access model—rather than comparing O(log n) with O(n) in isolation.

items.prompt: A random-access array is already sorted and receives one exact query. Both implementations are correct. Which asymptotic comparison applies?

options.text: Binary search is O(log n) and a worst-case scan is O(n).
Both are O(n).
The scan is O(1) because it may find target first.
Any midpoint loop is O(log n).

feedback.reason: When sorted order and random access already exist, binary search has the lower worst-case query cost.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
The one-query contrast changes if sorting, copying, or expensive predicate work must be added first.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A legal binary search halves n candidates to one in Θ(log n) checks. A scan may inspect all n positions, so its worst case is Θ(n) under the same O(1)-access model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_linear: The scan is linear, but legal half-discard leaves at most n/2^t candidates after t binary iterations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_constant: An early hit is best-case; an absent target or final-position hit still forces n inspections.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_without_invariant: A midpoint loop earns logarithmic time only when every branch legally removes a constant fraction and strictly progresses.

items.prompt: An unsorted random-access array receives one exact query. Which complete asymptotic comparison is correct?

options.text: A scan is O(n); sorting solely to enable binary search is O(n log n) overall.
Binary search is O(log n) on the unsorted array.
Sort plus binary search is O(log n) because only query time matters.
Both are O(log n).

feedback.reason: One-query strategy comparison includes the cost required to make each strategy legal.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
A direct scan is both correct and asymptotically cheaper than one-off sorting.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: For one request, scan totals Θ(n). Copying or sorting solely for binary search costs Θ(n log n) before its Θ(log n) lookup, so setup dominates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_log: Without order aligned to the query, a midpoint comparison cannot exclude either half and the search is incorrect.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_ignored: The sorted representation does not already exist, so its Θ(n log n) construction belongs to this one-query workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_log: A worst-case scan can inspect every one of n positions and therefore remains linear.

items.prompt: A sorted array has n = 6. Both a scan and binary search are correct. Which conclusion is defensible?

options.text: Binary search has better asymptotic worst case, but simplicity and measured constants may justify a scan for this tiny fixed size.
Binary search is mandatory because O(log n) always dominates engineering considerations.
The scan has the better asymptotic class.
Only one of the two is correct.

feedback.reason: Asymptotic advantage and practical preference are related but not identical.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
The transfer boundary is growth: binary search matters as n scales, while tiny fixed domains may favor simpler code.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Θ(log n) scales better than Θ(n), but with fixed n = 6 both perform only a handful of checks. Simplicity and measurement may therefore favor the scan without changing either asymptotic class.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_mandatory: Growth classes guide scaling but do not automatically outweigh code simplicity and constants for a tiny fixed domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_asymptotically_better: As n grows, linear inspections increase faster than logarithmic halvings, even if constants favor a small instance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.correctness_diff: Because the array is sorted and both algorithms check equality correctly, each satisfies the exact-match contract.

items.prompt: A scan stops at the first element and binary search takes several iterations. Does that make the scan asymptotically better for one successful input?

options.text: No. That is a favorable case for the scan, not its worst-case growth bound.
Yes. Linear scan is O(1) because one input finishes immediately.
Yes, and binary search is therefore incorrect.
Both always perform the same number of comparisons.

feedback.reason: Single-query cost comparison should distinguish best case, expected case, and worst case.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
A scan can be excellent on early hits while retaining O(n) worst-case behavior.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: The observed scan used its Θ(1) best case. Its worst case remains Θ(n), while binary search has Θ(log n) worst case; an expected comparison additionally needs a target distribution.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_o1: One favorable input demonstrates a best case but cannot bound every length-n input by constant work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_wrong: Taking several legal iterations affects performance on this instance and says nothing by itself about correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_always: Scan work varies with target position, while binary paths vary with comparisons and absence.

items.prompt: A sorted linked list receives one exact query. Which total-cost comparison is most accurate without extra indexing?

options.text: A sequential scan is O(n); repeatedly locating midpoints does not give ordinary O(log n) array-style binary search.
Binary search is automatically O(log n) because the values are sorted.
The scan is O(log n) because the list is sorted.
Both use O(1) extra space, so both are O(1) time.

feedback.reason: Data access cost is part of the strategy cost model.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Binary search becomes attractive after materializing or maintaining a random-access index, which is preprocessing.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A linked list lacks O(1) midpoint access. Repeatedly walking to successive midpoints costs linear aggregate traversal or worse, so sorted values alone do not provide array-style Θ(log n) lookup.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_log: The logarithmic comparison count omits the traversal required to reach each midpoint in a linked representation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_log: Sorted order may permit early stopping, but a target near the end or absent above all values still needs linear traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_constant: Constant auxiliary state does not imply constant time; the algorithms still traverse input-dependent numbers of nodes.

items.prompt: A sorted array query asks whether any value satisfies an arbitrary O(1) condition unrelated to the sort key. Which one-query method is correct?

options.text: Scan until a satisfying value is found or the array ends.
Binary-search the arbitrary condition because each check is O(1).
Check only the midpoint.
Sort again by the same key.

feedback.reason: For one query, correctness still precedes cost comparison.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
A separate index ordered by the queried property could move the boundary, but the existing sort does not.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Sorting by a different key gives no monotonic truth pattern for the arbitrary condition. Every unchecked position remains possible, so a scan is the canonical correct one-query method.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary: O(1) predicate cost reduces each check but does not create the monotonicity required to discard a side.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_only: A false midpoint leaves every other position possible, and a true midpoint may not satisfy a first/all-result contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_again: Sorting again by the same unrelated key preserves the same nonmonotonic predicate pattern.

items.prompt: A monotonic predicate search over W candidates calls an O(n) feasibility function. A direct O(n) algorithm solves the same one-query problem. Which is asymptotically cheaper?

options.text: The direct O(n) method, compared with O(n log W) for repeated predicate evaluation.
Binary search because it uses only O(log W) candidates.
They are always equal.
The result depends on the midpoint variable name.

feedback.reason: The full cost of one query includes every predicate evaluation.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Binary search saves candidate evaluations, but it may repeat expensive global work that a direct algorithm performs once.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Binary search performs Θ(log W) feasibility calls, each costing Θ(n), for Θ(n log W) total. The direct Θ(n) algorithm is asymptotically smaller for this one workload.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary: Reducing candidate count to log W does not erase the Θ(n) global work repeated at each candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.equal: The binary strategy multiplies Θ(n) by Θ(log W), whereas the direct method performs the linear work once.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unknown_without_mid: Midpoint variable spelling changes neither predicate cost nor the number of candidate evaluations.

items.prompt: An immutable unsorted input must remain in original order, but an O(n) additional copy is allowed. For one query, which strategy is asymptotically preferable?

options.text: Scan the original in O(n).
Copy, sort, and binary-search in O(n log n).
Sort the original in place.
Binary-search the unsorted original.

feedback.reason: Allowing a copy makes preprocessing legal but not necessarily economical.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
For one query, the scan avoids both O(n) extra storage and O(n log n) sorting work.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Scanning preserves order in Θ(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Copying then sorting is legal but costs Θ(n) space and Θ(n log n) time for a single lookup.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_sort_binary: The Θ(n log n) one-time sort dominates one Θ(log n) lookup and is asymptotically larger than scanning once.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_original: In-place sorting changes the required original order and therefore violates the immutable-input contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_original: The unsorted original provides no ordered implication for legal half-discard, so binary search is incorrect.

items.prompt: A sorted array query requires returning every occurrence of target. Which one-query cost statement is correct if k matches are output?

options.text: Boundary searches can locate the range in O(log n), but materializing k results still costs Ω(k).
The entire operation is O(log n) regardless of k.
A scan is O(n) and output has no additional cost.
Return one midpoint match because binary search is faster.

feedback.reason: A faster search phase does not remove output-sensitive lower bounds.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Binary search can still beat a full scan when k is small, but total time includes the emitted range.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Two boundary searches locate the matching interval in Θ(log n), but copying or emitting its k occurrences adds Θ(k). Total time is Θ(log n + k).

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pure_log: Locating boundaries logarithmically does not materialize the k records required by the result contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_always_n_only: A scan contributes Θ(n) discovery, and explicitly writing k results adds output work and storage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_match: Returning one occurrence changes an all-occurrences contract and is not a valid optimization.

items.prompt: A sorted array is stored remotely. Each random access has high network latency, while one sequential streaming pass is efficient. Which decision is justified?

options.text: Compare the real access model; a sequential scan may beat logarithmically many expensive random accesses.
Binary search is always faster because it makes fewer comparisons.
Scanning is always faster on remote data.
Use asymptotic classes without considering operation costs.

feedback.reason: Asymptotic operation counts assume a cost model for each access.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
When random and sequential accesses have radically different costs, one-query strategy may differ from the RAM model.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Binary search costs about L·log n in random-request latency, while streaming costs S(n). Compare those real expressions; neither comparison count alone nor the word 'remote' determines the winner.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_always: Fewer comparisons can still lose when each midpoint request pays high network round-trip latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_always: A remote index, cache or cheap range request may make logarithmic random access preferable under another access model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_latency: An asymptotic count is meaningful only after assigning costs to the actual random and sequential operations.

items.prompt: Which terms belong in a complete one-query comparison when data is initially unsorted? Select all that apply.

options.text: The cost of directly scanning the input.
Any copying and sorting needed to create a legal binary-search representation.
The binary-search query cost after preprocessing.
Benefits from unspecified future queries that are not part of the workload.

feedback.reason: A single-query model contains no automatic amortization over imagined future work.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
The entire legal path to the answer must be counted.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Count Θ(n) for the direct scan and the complete legal binary path: copy if required, Θ(n log n) sort, then Θ(log n) lookup. Unspecified future requests contribute zero reuse.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.future_queries: Amortizing setup over hypothetical requests understates the stated one-query workload and assumes reuse the contract never promises.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.query_cost: It remains part of the total.

items.prompt: Which conditions favor binary search for one query? Select all that apply.

options.text: The data is already sorted by the query key and supports random access.
A cheap predicate is proven monotonic over a large ordered candidate range.
n is large enough that the logarithmic reduction matters under the actual cost model.
The data is unsorted and the query condition is arbitrary.

feedback.reason: One-query binary search needs both legal structure and a workload where the reduced checks matter.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Unsorted arbitrary conditions stay on the scan side of the boundary.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Existing aligned random-access order or a cheap monotonic predicate makes half-discard legal; sufficiently large n and realistic access costs make fewer checks valuable. All conditions are workload facts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unsorted_arbitrary: Neither input order nor predicate monotonicity excludes a region, so a midpoint outcome cannot support correct binary elimination.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.already_sorted_random: No setup is required and half elimination is legal.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.large_n: Scale can make the asymptotic advantage material.

items.prompt: Which conditions favor a one-time scan? Select all that apply.

options.text: One query over unsorted data with no existing index.
The query condition is nonmonotonic in the available order.
The representation offers efficient sequential access but expensive midpoint access.
A large random-access array is already sorted by the query key.

feedback.reason: Scanning can win through lower setup cost, stronger correctness, or a better access pattern.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Existing aligned random-access order shifts the choice toward binary search.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A one-off unsorted query avoids index construction, a nonmonotonic condition requires individual checking, and sequential representations make a scan's access pattern cheaper. Existing large aligned order is the contrasting binary case.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stable_sorted_large: A large array already sorted by the query key with random access supplies both legal elimination and useful logarithmic reduction.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sequential_access: The physical access model favors scanning.

items.prompt: Which distinctions should be stated in a one-query performance claim? Select all that apply.

options.text: Best-case versus worst-case behavior.
Whether ordered data or an index already exists.
Random-access, comparison, and predicate costs.
Whether the implementation uses standard variable names.

feedback.reason: A meaningful comparison states the workload and cost model.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Otherwise “binary is faster” collapses several distinct cases into a slogan.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Best, expected and worst cases answer different guarantees; existing preprocessing changes the measured lifecycle; access and predicate costs determine what one iteration means. Variable names affect none of these.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Renaming left, right or mid changes no access, comparison, predicate evaluation, setup phase or iteration count.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.best_worst: Early scan success differs from absent-target cost.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.access_cost: The unit-cost RAM model may not apply.

items.prompt: Arrange the decision process for one exact query.

elements.text: State whether data is ordered, mutable, random-access, and query-aligned.
Discard strategies that cannot satisfy the result contract.
For each legal strategy, sum setup, access, predicate, query, and output work.
Choose the lower-cost or simpler legal strategy for this one query.

feedback.reason: Single-query analysis has no hidden future workload to amortize setup.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
The decision follows complete cost after correctness filtering.

items: State order, mutability, access model and alignment with the query.
Reject any strategy that cannot satisfy the exact result contract.
For each legal strategy, total setup, access, predicate, search and output work.
Choose the cheaper or simpler legal path for this one stated query.

blocks.text: Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Do not charge benefits to requests outside the workload. For q = 1, every required setup term is paid by that one answer.

items.prompt: Arrange the analysis of an early-exit scan versus binary search.

elements.text: State whether the claim concerns best, average, or worst case.
Count scan inspections under that case distribution.
Count legal binary-search iterations and access costs.
Compare both strategies under the same case and cost model.

feedback.reason: Comparing the scan best case with binary-search worst case is not a valid general conclusion.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Both strategies must be evaluated under aligned assumptions.

items: Choose best, expected or worst case and state any distribution.
Count scan inspections under that selected case.
Count legal binary iterations and the real cost of each access or predicate.
Compare both totals under the same case, representation and cost model.

blocks.text: Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: An early scan hit can be compared with a binary instance trace, but it cannot support a general worst-case or expected strategy claim.

items.prompt: One exact query is made on an unsorted array. Strategy A scans. Strategy B copies, sorts, and binary-searches. Select total time and additional space.
constraints: Comparison sorting is O(n log n).
The sorted copy occupies O(n) space.

feedback.reason: The one-query binary strategy pays setup in both time and memory.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Strategy A inspects at most n elements and retains only a cursor, so time is O(n) and auxiliary space O(1). Strategy B copies n elements in O(n) time and O(n) space, sorts the copy in O(n log n), then searches in O(log n); total time simplifies to O(n log n) and additional space remains O(n).
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: The comparison is scan O(n)/O(1) versus copy-sort-search O(n log n)/O(n). One logarithmic query cannot erase the legal representation it required.

items.prompt: A sorted random-access array receives one exact query. Select worst-case time and auxiliary space for iterative binary search and linear scan.
constraints: Neither materializes output beyond one index or boolean.

feedback.reason: Existing legal order exposes the pure query-cost contrast.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

With existing sorted random access, iterative binary search halves the interval and takes O(log n) worst-case time with O(1) auxiliary state. Linear scan may examine all n elements and takes O(n) time, also with O(1) auxiliary state.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: No preprocessing term appears because the prompt places sorted random-access data outside the query workload. The difference is therefore O(log n) versus O(n), not setup.

items.prompt: A monotonic candidate search has range width W and predicate cost P(n). A direct algorithm answers the same query in D(n). Select the binary-search total and the comparison rule.
constraints: The binary search performs O(log W) predicate evaluations.

feedback.reason: The one-query choice depends on full algorithmic work, not the outer loop alone.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Binary search evaluates the predicate O(log W) times, and each evaluation costs P(n), so its total is O(P(n)·log W). The direct algorithm costs D(n). Choose binary only when its full expression is lower under the same model; legality alone does not make it faster.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Compare P(n)·log W with D(n), including setup and output if either strategy needs them. Counting only logarithmic candidate checks hides predicate work.

items.prompt: A sorted dataset is streamed sequentially from remote storage. One sequential pass costs S(n), while each random midpoint request costs L and binary search makes O(log n) such requests. Select the two cost expressions.
constraints: Ignore local computation relative to access cost.

feedback.reason: The preferred strategy depends on whether S(n) is smaller or larger than L log n.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The sequential strategy pays S(n) for one pass. Binary search makes O(log n) random requests at cost L each, for O(L log n). Choose by comparing S(n) with L log n, not by comparing n with log n while pretending both access types cost one.
Contrast the strategies

Compare total work for the stated workload, not only the search loop. Binary search is attractive when sorted random-access data already exists; a scan can be preferable when sorting, copying, traversal, or predicate evaluation must first be paid for.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Remote latency belongs inside the symbolic bound: scan = S(n), binary = L·log n. Caching, batching or a local index would define a different model.
